questions.q: A Chilean label carries a Denominación de Origen. Under the Court's reading of the DO system, what does that name control?
opts: Where the grapes were grown, and nothing more
The grapes permitted and a ceiling on yield
A minimum period of ageing in oak
Approval by a blind tasting panel
questions.exp: The Court describes Chile's Denominación de Origen as a statement of geographic origin only, with no further rules: no grape list, no yield limit, no ageing requirement and no tasting panel. Label words such as Reserva and the percentage rules for variety, vintage and origin sit in separate national labelling rules, not in the DO itself.

questions.q: Chile's DO system nests four tiers of place. Running from the largest, they begin Region, Subregion and Zone; name the smallest tier.
questions.exp: Decreto 464 maps Chilean origin from the Región vitícola down through the Subregión, usually a valley such as the Maipo, and the Zona, such as Colchagua within Rapel, to the Área, usually a single commune such as Puente Alto or Peumo. The Court names the four tiers Region, Subregion, Zone and Area.

questions.q: Chilean law asks 75 per cent for a stated variety, vintage or origin. What share must each reach on wine shipped to the European Union?
questions.exp: The Court's Certified line sets Chile's own minimum at 75 per cent for variety, vintage and origin, and notes that the European Union requires 85 per cent in all three, so most export wine is made to the higher figure. The 75 per cent rule is Chile's domestic floor; Argentina, Australia and New Zealand work to 85 per cent at home.

questions.q: The Court credits the Valle Central DO, Chile's warm trough running from the Maipo south to the Maule, with roughly what share of the country's wine production?
questions.exp: The Court gives the Valle Central about 80 per cent of Chilean production: a warm to hot trough holding the Maipo, Rapel, Curicó and Maule valleys and the country's volume Cabernet Sauvignon, Carménère and Merlot. A blend drawn from more than one of those valleys falls back to the Valle Central name on its label.

questions.q: Chile created a special denomination under the name Secano Interior for wines from the dry-farmed communes of the southern Coastal Range. Beside Cinsault, which red grape was it established for?
questions.exp: The Secano Interior denomination was created for País and Cinsault grown in listed dry-farmed communes of the southern Coastal Range, the heart of Chile's old-vine revival. País, the colonial grape known as Listán Prieto in Spain and Mission in California, is a Certified red on the Court's list beside Syrah; Maule's old dry-farmed Carignan carries the private VIGNO seal instead.

questions.q: Founded in 1994 by the French family behind Grand Marnier, which house on the Court's Chilean list made its name in Colchagua?
questions.exp: Casa Lapostolle was founded in 1994 by the Marnier-Lapostolle family of Grand Marnier, and its Clos Apalta, a Carménère-led blend from old hillside vines in the Apalta horseshoe of Colchagua, is the country's best-known Carménère icon. Errázuriz belongs to Aconcagua, while Santa Rita and Concha y Toro are nineteenth-century houses of the Maipo.

questions.q: Founded in 1850 at Alto Jahuel in the Maipo, which house on the Court's list claims the oldest brand in Chilean wine?
questions.exp: Viña Carmen, founded in 1850 beside Santa Rita at Alto Jahuel, claims the oldest brand in Chilean wine and bottled one of the first wines sold as Carménère after the grape was identified in 1994. The Court's Certified list sets it beside Concha y Toro, Santa Rita, Errázuriz and Casa Lapostolle.

questions.q: In the 1600s, what held back wine production in Spain's South American colonies, as the Court's history of Chile records?
opts: A Church ban on new vineyards
questions.exp: The Spanish crown, protecting the trade in wine shipped from Spain, issued decrees restricting new planting in its American colonies, though distance meant they were widely ignored and vineyards spread regardless. The Court's timeline runs on from vines in the 1500s to expansion after independence and European immigration in the 1800s, and foreign investment in the 1970s and 1980s; phylloxera has never reached Chile.
